fn.en: Talk about future plans and predictions.

tts: How do you think our working lives will change in the future?

Life is changing pretty fast, and the world of work will change with it. In many countries populations are ageing. This means there will probably be more jobs in the healthcare sector, but it also means a smaller workforce overall.

For one thing, we are likely to have more and more automation. Trains and buses probably will not have drivers any more. Instead we will have self-driving vehicles and a handful of humans acting as auto transport analysts.
So IT skills will be important? — Certainly, but I do not think we will see them as specific skills in the future. Pretty much everyone will have them, just as they can read and write nowadays.

Another factor that will lead to new jobs is the environment. You might become a garbage designer — somebody who designs products from what we currently throw away. Or a rewilder, who undoes environmental damage by replanting and reintroducing native species.

items.q: What is the interview about?
o: How work is likely to change, and what jobs may appear

items.q: What does the consultant say about IT skills?
o: They will stop being seen as specific skills, because everybody will have them

items.q: What is a rewilder?
o: Somebody who undoes environmental damage by replanting

tts: Ben: When I was a kid I always wanted to be a train driver. I am not sure any of those jobs would be for me, but I completely agree that IT skills are going to be vital. My skills are not bad, but I am nearly thirty and I am well aware that younger generations are going to be much more proficient. So I am taking a course in app design at the University of Westminster. It starts next week and I am really excited.
Lucy: I am studying design, so I might quite fancy being a garbage designer. I am certainly going to work in design in some way.

John: How about being a nostalgist? Another big trend is customization — providing goods and services tailored to what individuals want. Nostalgists will be interior designers who specialize in recreating a particular time in the past.

A third speaker: I am in my third year at university, which means that I graduate this summer, assuming I pass. There is a lot of unemployment at the moment, so it is probably going to be quite hard to get a good job straightaway. I am going to work in my parents’ shop over the summer, and then in September I am planning on visiting a friend in Vancouver.

items.q: “I’m taking a course. It starts next week.” What kind of future is this?
o: A fixed arrangement — it is already booked

items.q: “IT skills are going to be vital.” Why going to rather than will?
o: The speaker is predicting from evidence he can already see

items.q: “There will probably be more jobs in healthcare.” What kind of future?
o: A prediction based on the speaker’s own judgement

items.q: “I’m going to work in my parents’ shop.” What does going to signal here?

acts.title: Three futures, and what separates them
rule: English has no future tense. It has several present forms pressed into future service, and each carries a different message about how settled the future is. The choice is not about time — all three refer to the future — but about where the future currently lives: in a diary, in a decision, or in your head.
points: A fixed arrangement. Somebody else is involved, or it is written down. I’m seeing the dentist at four.
A decision already taken, or a prediction from evidence you can see right now.
A prediction from your own opinion, a decision made at the moment of speaking, an offer or a promise.
Timetables only: the train leaves at six, the course starts on Monday.
probably goes after will and before won’t: I’ll probably go / I probably won’t go.
eg: I’m taking a course in app design.
Arrangement — enrolled, paid for, in the diary.
The course starts next week.
Timetable — present simple.
I’m going to work in my parents’ shop this summer.
Decision already taken.
Look at those figures — it’s going to be a difficult year.
Prediction from present evidence.
I think there will be more jobs in healthcare.
Prediction from opinion.
That’s the phone. I’ll get it.
Decision made while speaking.
I’ll send you the file tonight, I promise.
A promise.
Younger generations are going to be much more proficient.
Evidence-based prediction.
I’ll probably apply, but I haven’t decided.
probably after will.
I probably won’t apply this year.
probably before won’t.
acts.careful: “I will take a course next week” is not wrong English, but it says something different: it makes the course sound like a decision you have just this second reached. If it is booked, use the present continuous.

write.q: Write about 180 words on the next two years of your working or studying life. Separate the three futures clearly: at least two fixed arrangements in the present continuous, at least two decisions with going to, and at least two predictions with will. Hedge the predictions properly.
plan: what you have decided but not yet booked
what you predict about your field
what you are least sure of
write.model:
Over the next two years two things are already fixed. I am starting a part-time course in data analysis in October — it runs for eleven months and the first payment has gone. And I am moving offices in January, which is not my decision but is definitely happening.

Beyond that it is decisions rather than arrangements. I am going to stop taking on evening work, which I have said before and this time have written down. I am also going to apply for one internal role, whether or not I get it.

As for predictions, I think the reporting side of my job will disappear within three years. Not because anybody plans it, but because two of the four systems already do it themselves. I expect we will keep the title and lose the work.

What I am least sure of is whether I will still want it. I probably will. But I would not have said that about the last job either.
